passages.title: Crowds and healing do not confine the message to one town
passages.summary: Mark begins with John the Baptist preaching in the desert. Jesus is baptized, and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son. He is tested in the desert for forty days. He announces that God’s Kingdom is near and calls four fishermen. In Capernaum he teaches with authority and drives out an unclean spirit. He heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others at the door. Before dawn he goes out alone to pray. He then leaves for other towns and heals a man with a skin disease.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: Why does Jesus leave the gathered crowd to visit other towns?

contextNote.title: Crowds and healing do not confine the message to one town
contextNote.text: By the evening of verse 33 the whole town is at the door. Jesus has healed many. Before dawn he leaves to pray alone (verse 35). The disciples find him and say everyone is looking for him. Verse 38 gives his answer: “Let’s go elsewhere.” He came to preach, and other towns have not heard. Success in one place does not decide where he goes next.

passages.title: A blocked doorway leads into disputes about authority and need
passages.summary: Four men carry a paralyzed man to Jesus and lower him through the roof. Jesus forgives his sins and heals him. He calls Levi the tax collector and eats with sinners. He is asked why his disciples do not fast. He says no one puts new wine into old wineskins. On a Sabbath his disciples pick grain as they walk. Pharisees object, and he recalls what David did when hungry. He says the Sabbath was made for people.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the carriers’ faith and shared help. How does the Sabbath answer connect its purpose with human need?

contextNote.title: A blocked doorway leads into disputes about authority and need
contextNote.text: Each scene in this chapter raises a complaint. Jesus forgives, eats with sinners, and does not have his disciples fast. The last complaint is about picking grain on the Sabbath. Verse 25 answers with David’s need and hunger. Verse 27 then states the purpose of the day. The Sabbath was made for people’s good. A rule about rest should not be turned against the hungry.

passages.title: The question about saving life exposes the plan to destroy it
passages.summary: Jesus enters a synagogue where a man has a withered hand. His opponents watch to see whether he will heal on the Sabbath. He asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, saving life or killing. They say nothing, and he heals the man. The Pharisees begin to plot his death. Crowds press on him, and he appoints twelve to be with him. Scribes say he drives out demons by their ruler. He says those who do God’s will are his family.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson uses the divided house saying to teach unity. How does the question about saving life expose the opponents’ plan?

contextNote.title: The question about saving life exposes the plan to destroy it
contextNote.text: The watchers in verse 2 hope to accuse Jesus. Verse 4 puts a question to them with two pairs. Is the Sabbath for doing good or harm, for saving life or killing? They stay silent. He heals the man, which is the good. Verse 6 shows what they do on that same Sabbath. They go out and plan how to destroy him.

passages.title: Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat
passages.summary: Jesus teaches a large crowd from a boat. A farmer sows seed on path, rock, thorns, and good soil. He explains the story to his disciples in private. A lamp is meant to be set on a stand. Seed grows by itself while the farmer sleeps. The Kingdom is like a tiny mustard seed that becomes a large plant. That evening a storm fills the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind, and the disciples are terrified.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson reads the storm account through peace during trouble. Why does fear remain after the disciples hear explanations and see the storm stop?

contextNote.title: Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat
contextNote.text: The disciples have spent the day hearing about trust in a hidden Kingdom. That night the waves break into the boat. Verse 38 gives their question: does he not care that they are dying? They doubt his concern, not his power. He stills the storm and asks why they have no faith (verse 40). Verse 41 says they were then even more afraid. They ask who this can be.

passages.title: One healing interrupts another urgent request
passages.summary: Jesus crosses the lake and frees a man held by many demons. The man had lived among tombs, and no chain could hold him. The townspeople beg Jesus to leave. Jairus, a synagogue leader, begs him to come to his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak. She is healed, and Jesus stops to find her. Word comes that the girl has died. Jesus takes her hand, and she gets up.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: Why does Jesus stop to hear the woman while Jairus waits?

contextNote.title: One healing interrupts another urgent request
contextNote.text: A leader’s daughter is dying, and every moment counts. A woman in the crowd touches Jesus and is healed at once (verse 29). He could have kept walking. He stops and asks who touched him (verse 30). She comes forward in fear and tells him everything. Verse 34 calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace. She receives his attention as well as her cure, while Jairus waits.

passages.title: The loaves should have changed the disciples' response to the sea
passages.summary: Jesus teaches in his home town, and the people take offense. He sends the twelve out two by two. Herod has John the Baptist beheaded after a rash promise at a feast. The twelve return, and Jesus takes them aside to rest. A crowd follows, and he feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish. That night he walks on the sea toward the disciples’ boat. They are terrified, and he gets in with them. People bring the sick wherever he goes.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: What should the disciples have understood from the loaves before the sea encounter?

contextNote.title: The loaves should have changed the disciples' response to the sea
contextNote.text: The disciples have just handed out bread to thousands (verses 41–43). Hours later they see Jesus on the water and cry out in fear. Verse 52 explains their reaction. They had not understood about the loaves. The feeding should have shown them who was with them. Their hearts were hardened. In Mark the people closest to Jesus are often slow to see.

passages.title: A sacred gift claim can hide neglected parents
passages.summary: Pharisees ask why Jesus’s disciples eat with unwashed hands. He says they honor God with their lips and hold to human tradition. The law says to honor father and mother. They let a man declare his goods “Corban,” a gift to God. He then gives his parents nothing. Jesus says evil comes from within, out of the heart. He heals a foreign woman’s daughter. He opens the ears and mouth of a deaf man.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How can calling property sacred become a refusal to help parents?

contextNote.title: A sacred gift claim can hide neglected parents
contextNote.text: “Corban” in verse 11 means something pledged to God. A man could say this about the support he owed his parents. Verse 12 states the result. He is then not allowed to do anything for his father or mother. A religious vow cancels a plain commandment. Jesus says this makes God’s word void (verse 13). The example shows how piety can excuse neglect.

passages.title: Partial sight stands beside partial understanding
passages.summary: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves. Pharisees ask for a sign, and he refuses. In the boat the disciples worry that they have one loaf. He asks whether they still do not understand. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. He asks who they say he is, and Peter calls him the Christ. Jesus says he must suffer, and Peter rebukes him. Jesus says his followers must take up their cross.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does the two-stage healing sit beside Peter’s incomplete understanding?

contextNote.title: Partial sight stands beside partial understanding
contextNote.text: This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two steps. After the first touch the man sees people like walking trees (verse 24). After the second he sees clearly (verse 25). Mark places the story between two scenes of poor sight. The disciples fail to understand the loaves (verses 17–21). Peter then names Jesus rightly and rejects his suffering (verses 29–32). Their sight is also partial.

passages.title: The father's request admits the weakness that disciples conceal
passages.summary: Jesus is changed in appearance on a mountain before three disciples. A voice from the cloud tells them to listen to him. Below, a father has brought a son whom the disciples could not heal. The father asks Jesus to help if he can. Jesus says all things are possible for one who believes. The father cries that he believes and asks help for his unbelief. Jesus heals the boy and again foretells his death. The disciples argue about who is greatest.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does the father’s request differ from the disciples’ silence about their fears?

contextNote.title: The father's request admits the weakness that disciples conceal
contextNote.text: The father’s cry in verse 24 holds two things together. He believes, and he knows his belief is weak. He says both aloud and asks for help. The disciples behave differently in this chapter. They do not understand and are afraid to ask (verse 32). They argue about rank and fall silent when questioned (verse 34). The father admits his weakness, and they hide theirs.

passages.title: The same question reveals different desires in two requests
passages.summary: Jesus teaches about marriage and blesses the children. A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and leaves in sorrow. Jesus foretells his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left in glory. He says whoever would be great must be a servant. At Jericho a blind beggar named Bartimaeus cries out to him. Jesus asks what he wants. He asks to see, receives his sight, and follows Jesus.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the wealthy man’s question about following Jesus. How do the two answers to the same question reveal different desires?

contextNote.title: The same question reveals different desires in two requests
contextNote.text: Jesus asks the same question twice in this chapter. In verse 36 he asks James and John what they want. They ask for the seats of honor. In verse 51 he asks a blind beggar. The beggar asks to see. One request seeks rank, and the other seeks sight. Verse 52 says the beggar then followed Jesus on the road.

passages.title: The fig tree surrounds a dispute about the temple's purpose
passages.summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt, and people shout “Hosanna.” The next day he finds a fig tree with leaves and no fruit. He says no one will eat from it again. He drives the buyers and sellers out of the temple. He says God’s house should be a house of prayer for all nations. The following morning the fig tree has withered. He teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness. The leaders ask by what authority he does these things.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How do the tree scenes frame the temple interruption?

contextNote.title: The fig tree surrounds a dispute about the temple's purpose
contextNote.text: Mark wraps the temple scene inside the fig tree story. The tree is cursed in verses 12–14 and found dead in verses 20–21. Between them Jesus stops the temple’s trade. Verse 17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The house was meant for the prayer of all nations. A tree with leaves and no fruit frames that charge. The show of life without its purpose is what is judged.

passages.title: The widow's whole living follows a warning about consumed houses
passages.summary: Jesus tells of tenants who kill a vineyard owner’s son. He is asked about paying taxes to Caesar and about the resurrection. A scribe asks which commandment is first. Jesus names love of God and love of neighbor. He warns about scribes who love honor and devour widows’ houses. He sits and watches people put money in the temple treasury. Rich people give large sums. A poor widow gives two small coins, all she has.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does the warning about widows’ houses affect reading the widow’s gift?

contextNote.title: The widow's whole living follows a warning about consumed houses
contextNote.text: Verse 40 warns of scribes who “devour widows’ houses.” The next scene shows a widow at the treasury. Verse 44 says she gave everything she had to live on. Jesus praises the size of her gift measured by her means. The warning just before should stay in the reader’s mind. A system that takes a widow’s last coins is also in view. The next chapter opens with the temple’s coming ruin (13:2).

passages.title: The warning to watch does not supply a predictable hour
passages.summary: A disciple admires the temple’s great stones. Jesus says not one will be left on another. Four disciples ask when this will happen. He warns of deceivers, wars, earthquakes, and trials before councils. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come in the clouds. No one knows the day or the hour. They must stay awake, like servants whose master is away.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: What work remains possible when the day and hour stay unknown?

contextNote.title: The warning to watch does not supply a predictable hour
contextNote.text: The disciples ask for timing and a sign (verse 4). Verse 32 says no one knows the day, not even the Son. So the chapter cannot be used as a timetable. Verse 34 gives a different picture. A man leaves home and gives each servant his work. The doorkeeper is told to watch. The command to stay awake is a command to keep at one’s task.

passages.title: The woman's understood gift contrasts with failed promises
passages.summary: The leaders look for a way to arrest Jesus. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head. Some scold her, and Jesus defends her. Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover and gives the bread and the cup. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish while his friends sleep. He is arrested, and all the disciples run. The council condemns him, and Peter denies him three times.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: How does the woman’s action differ from the disciples’ promises?

contextNote.title: The woman's understood gift contrasts with failed promises
contextNote.text: Some at the table call the woman’s gift a waste (verses 4–5). Verse 8 gives Jesus’s reading of it. She has done what she could and prepared his body for burial. She alone acts as if his death is near. The disciples make promises in this chapter. Peter swears he will die before denying him (verse 31). By verse 50 they have all fled.

passages.title: Mocked kingship becomes recognition beside the cross
passages.summary: The council hands Jesus to Pilate. Pilate offers to release him, and the crowd chooses Barabbas. Soldiers dress Jesus in purple and mock him as king. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross. He is crucified with two robbers, and passersby mock him. Darkness covers the land, and he cries out and dies. The temple curtain tears in two. A Roman officer says this man was the Son of God.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: Why does the officer’s recognition follow death rather than escape from the cross?

contextNote.title: Mocked kingship becomes recognition beside the cross
contextNote.text: Mockers tell Jesus to come down from the cross so they can believe (verse 32). He does not come down. Verse 39 says the officer saw how he died. The officer then calls him Son of God. This is the first human in Mark to say so. He is a foreign soldier at an execution. Recognition comes at the death, not through an escape from it.

passages.title: The message names Peter after his denial and the disciples' flight
passages.summary: After the Sabbath three women bring spices to the tomb. They wonder who will roll away the stone. They find it moved and a young man in white inside. He says Jesus has risen and is not there. They must tell his disciples and Peter that he goes ahead to Galilee. The women flee, trembling and afraid. The longer ending tells of Jesus appearing to Mary Magdalene and others. He sends the eleven into all the world.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers separate named settings from remembered places. Exact houses, tombs, unnamed mountains, and travel routes remain unassigned.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches resurrection through the Gospel accounts. Why does the tomb message name Peter after his denial?

contextNote.title: The message names Peter after his denial and the disciples' flight
contextNote.text: The disciples fled at the arrest (14:50). Peter denied Jesus three times (14:66–72). Verse 7 sends a message to “his disciples and Peter.” Peter is named on his own. The one who failed most publicly is not left out. The message also promises a meeting in Galilee, as Jesus said (14:28). The first word to those who ran is an invitation back.

events.title: The same question reveals different desires in two requests
events.summary: Jesus teaches about marriage and blesses the children. A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and leaves in sorrow. Jesus foretells his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left in glory. He says whoever would be great must be a servant. At Jericho a blind beggar named Bartimaeus cries out to him. Jesus asks what he wants. He asks to see, receives his sight, and follows Jesus.
events.detail: Jesus asks the same question twice in this chapter. In verse 36 he asks James and John what they want. They ask for the seats of honor. In verse 51 he asks a blind beggar. The beggar asks to see. One request seeks rank, and the other seeks sight. Verse 52 says the beggar then followed Jesus on the road.

events.title: The fig tree surrounds a dispute about the temple's purpose
events.summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt, and people shout “Hosanna.” The next day he finds a fig tree with leaves and no fruit. He says no one will eat from it again. He drives the buyers and sellers out of the temple. He says God’s house should be a house of prayer for all nations. The following morning the fig tree has withered. He teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness. The leaders ask by what authority he does these things.
events.detail: Mark wraps the temple scene inside the fig tree story. The tree is cursed in verses 12–14 and found dead in verses 20–21. Between them Jesus stops the temple’s trade. Verse 17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The house was meant for the prayer of all nations. A tree with leaves and no fruit frames that charge. The show of life without its purpose is what is judged.

events.title: The widow's whole living follows a warning about consumed houses

events.title: The warning to watch does not supply a predictable hour
events.summary: A disciple admires the temple’s great stones. Jesus says not one will be left on another. Four disciples ask when this will happen. He warns of deceivers, wars, earthquakes, and trials before councils. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come in the clouds. No one knows the day or the hour. They must stay awake, like servants whose master is away.
events.detail: The disciples ask for timing and a sign (verse 4). Verse 32 says no one knows the day, not even the Son. So the chapter cannot be used as a timetable. Verse 34 gives a different picture. A man leaves home and gives each servant his work. The doorkeeper is told to watch. The command to stay awake is a command to keep at one’s task.

events.title: The woman's understood gift contrasts with failed promises
events.summary: The leaders look for a way to arrest Jesus. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head. Some scold her, and Jesus defends her. Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover and gives the bread and the cup. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish while his friends sleep. He is arrested, and all the disciples run. The council condemns him, and Peter denies him three times.
events.detail: Some at the table call the woman’s gift a waste (verses 4–5). Verse 8 gives Jesus’s reading of it. She has done what she could and prepared his body for burial. She alone acts as if his death is near. The disciples make promises in this chapter. Peter swears he will die before denying him (verse 31). By verse 50 they have all fled.

events.title: Mocked kingship becomes recognition beside the cross
events.summary: The council hands Jesus to Pilate. Pilate offers to release him, and the crowd chooses Barabbas. Soldiers dress Jesus in purple and mock him as king. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross. He is crucified with two robbers, and passersby mock him. Darkness covers the land, and he cries out and dies. The temple curtain tears in two. A Roman officer says this man was the Son of God.
events.detail: Mockers tell Jesus to come down from the cross so they can believe (verse 32). He does not come down. Verse 39 says the officer saw how he died. The officer then calls him Son of God. This is the first human in Mark to say so. He is a foreign soldier at an execution. Recognition comes at the death, not through an escape from it.

events.title: The message names Peter after his denial and the disciples' flight
events.summary: After the Sabbath three women bring spices to the tomb. They wonder who will roll away the stone. They find it moved and a young man in white inside. He says Jesus has risen and is not there. They must tell his disciples and Peter that he goes ahead to Galilee. The women flee, trembling and afraid. The longer ending tells of Jesus appearing to Mary Magdalene and others. He sends the eleven into all the world.
events.detail: The disciples fled at the arrest (14:50). Peter denied Jesus three times (14:66–72). Verse 7 sends a message to “his disciples and Peter.” Peter is named on his own. words.label: Covenant
words.meaning: A binding agreement with promises and duties. In the Bible, God makes covenants with people.

words.label: Sabbath
words.meaning: The seventh day of the week, kept as a day of rest.

words.label: Gentiles
words.meaning: People of nations other than Israel.

words.label: Pharisees
words.meaning: A Jewish group known for careful keeping of the law. Acts 23:8 says they believed in resurrection, angels, and spirits.

words.label: Sadducees
words.meaning: A Jewish group close to the high priest (Acts 5:17). Acts 23:8 says they denied resurrection, angels, and spirits.

words.label: Scribes
words.meaning: People trained to write and to keep records. In the Gospels, scribes also teach the law.

words.label: Synagogue
words.meaning: A local Jewish meeting place for prayer and for reading Scripture.

words.label: Apostles
words.meaning: People sent out with a message. In the Gospels the word names twelve whom Jesus chose.

words.label: Passover
words.meaning: A yearly feast that recalls Israel’s escape from Egypt. Exodus 12 gives its first account.

words.label: Unclean
words.meaning: Unfit to take part in worship until a set cleansing is done. Leviticus 11–15 gives the rules.

words.label: Leprosy
words.meaning: A skin disease. Leviticus 13 uses the word for several conditions and sets rules for them.

words.label: Anoint
words.meaning: To pour oil on a person or thing to set it apart. Kings and priests were anointed.

words.label: Rabbi
words.meaning: A title of respect for a teacher. John 1:38 gives the meaning as “Teacher.”

words.label: Parable
words.meaning: A short story or comparison that teaches a point.

words.label: Centurion
words.meaning: A Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers.

words.label: Denarius
words.meaning: A Roman silver coin. Matthew 20:2 gives it as a worker’s pay for one day.

words.label: Abba
words.meaning: An Aramaic word for father. The text gives the translation beside it.

words.label: Yeast
words.meaning: Yeast, or leaven, makes dough rise. Bread made without it is called unleavened.

guides.title: Mark: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat
steps.text: The disciples have spent the day hearing about trust in a hidden Kingdom. That night the waves break into the boat. Verse 38 gives their question: does he not care that they are dying? They doubt his concern, not his power. He stills the storm and asks why they have no faith (verse 40). Verse 41 says they were then even more afraid. They ask who this can be.

steps.title: Partial sight stands beside partial understanding
steps.text: This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two steps. After the first touch the man sees people like walking trees (verse 24). After the second he sees clearly (verse 25). Mark places the story between two scenes of poor sight. The disciples fail to understand the loaves (verses 17–21). Peter then names Jesus rightly and rejects his suffering (verses 29–32). Their sight is also partial.

chapterMaps.narrative: Mark begins with John the Baptist preaching in the desert. Jesus is baptized, and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son. He is tested in the desert for forty days. He announces that God’s Kingdom is near and calls four fishermen. In Capernaum he teaches with authority and drives out an unclean spirit. He heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others at the door. Before dawn he goes out alone to pray. He then leaves for other towns and heals a man with a skin disease.

He is asked why his disciples do not fast. He says no one puts new wine into old wineskins. On a Sabbath his disciples pick grain as they walk. Pharisees object, and he recalls what David did when hungry. He says the Sabbath was made for people.

He asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, saving life or killing. They say nothing, and he heals the man. The Pharisees begin to plot his death. Crowds press on him, and he appoints twelve to be with him. Scribes say he drives out demons by their ruler. He says those who do God’s will are his family.
